Eighteen of his scores went up — more than anyone. But Hunting is the only place where the team average rose and his fell. Almost everything he closed came from the book he inherited or from people who called in, and the deals that stalled all stalled the same way: one contact who left, went on leave, or stopped answering.

Your move
  1. Give him a weekly activity number — dials and drop-bys. He's the only rep who's never had one. He can't control who answers; he can control how many times he goes.
  2. Require a second named contact in every open account. That's the fix for the stalls, and it's mechanical.
  3. Revisit his goal board. It's from May 2025 and most of it is already done, which is usually why Commitment slides.

He has the best Reaching Decision-Makers score on the team now — the only rep who improved there. The training took. What didn't hold is the drive behind it, and no tactic fixes that. Worth naming out loud: he's the only one who wasn't handed a book. Seth inherited Oregon, Jared inherited Washington, AJ built Idaho from about $300K against an $840K number.

Your move
  1. Finish the role decision. Full-time sales or not — it's been open since last October and he was still getting pulled onto installs.
  2. Build the structure his profile has always called for. He executes when you're in the car; the scores say it doesn't hold when you're not. That's a setting, not a character flaw.
  3. Point him at smaller, faster deals for a quarter. He needs a win cycle, not another six-month elephant.

He committed to 40 calls a week and hit it two weeks running — that's the Commitment jump from 5 to 81, and it's real. The trade-off is that he's booking meetings faster than he's qualifying them. He said it himself before he saw any score: chasing the meeting count means the math stops working. His activity mix backs it up — LinkedIn and email are high, self-initiated calls and walk-ins are near zero.

Your move
  1. Change what you count. Qualified meetings, not meetings. Ask him for the compelling reason to buy before you ask how many he booked.
  2. Make him cut the open pipeline down. 124 open deals means none of them gets real attention.
  3. He's now asking who the decision-maker is — you confirmed that in April. He still isn't in the room with them. That's the ceiling on his number.

Three Changes

Starting Monday
  1. Put an activity number on the Monday board for all three — dials, drop-bys, walk-ins. Seth included, especially Seth. Activity is what they control; conversations and meetings are the yield.
  2. Ask one qualification question in every deal review: what's the compelling reason to buy, and who signs?
  3. Run one pipeline debrief a month. Three lost deals, one question — what happened at the end?
